claim: YAP/TAZ promote proliferation of immature Schwann cells in developing peripheral nerves.
source: Consistent with this role, we and others have recently shown that YAP/TAZ promote vigorous proliferation of immature Schwann cells (SC) in developing peripheral nerves (Poitelon et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Poitelon et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017).

claim: Overexpression of YAP/TAZ promotes abnormally excessive proliferation of mature SCs in adult peripheral nerves.
source: overexpression of YAP/TAZ promotes abnormally excessive proliferation of mature SCs in adult peripheral nerves (Mindos et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Mindos et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018).

claim: YAP or YAP/TAZ promote differentiation of developing SCs by upregulating myelin-associated genes.
source: several groups demonstrated that YAP or YAP/TAZ promote differentiation of developing SCs by upregulating myelin-associated genes, thereby mediating developmental myelination (Fernando et al., 2016; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016; Poitelon et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five published studies (Fernando et al., 2016; Lopez-Anido et al., 2016; Poitelon et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017).

claim: YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed in differentiated myelin-forming SCs.
source: Our group additionally showed that YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed in differentiated myelin-forming SCs, and that they are required for maintenance of the myelin sheath in adult nerves (Grove et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Grove et al., 2017).

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for maintenance of the myelin sheath in adult nerves.
source: Our group additionally showed that YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed in differentiated myelin-forming SCs, and that they are required for maintenance of the myelin sheath in adult nerves (Grove et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Grove et al., 2017).

claim: YAP/TAZ are nuclear and transcriptionally active in mature SCs maintaining peripheral myelination.
source: We were therefore intrigued to find that YAP/TAZ are nuclear and transcriptionally active in mature SCs maintaining peripheral myelination.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous findings, as indicated by the context.

claim: Following traumatic nerve injury, SCs in axotomized nerve rapidly dedifferentiate and proliferate as they convert to regeneration promoting 'repair' SCs.
source: Following traumatic nerve injury, SCs in axotomized nerve rapidly dedifferentiate and proliferate as they convert to regeneration promoting 'repair' SCs (Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Tricaud and Park, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Tricaud and Park, 2017).

claim: When repair SCs regain axon contacts, they re-differentiate to myelin-forming SCs, thereby restoring motor and sensory functions.
source: When repair SCs regain axon contacts, they re-differentiate to myelin-forming SCs, thereby restoring motor and sensory functions (Fex Svennigsen and Dahlin, 2013; Stassart et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Fex Svennigsen and Dahlin, 2013; Stassart et al., 2013).

claim: YAP/TAZ disappear from denervated SCs but reappear in SCs as axons regenerate.
source: Strikingly, we found that YAP/TAZ disappear from denervated SCs but reappear in SCs as axons regenerate.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: YAP/TAZ are dispensable for SC proliferation after injury.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that YAP/TAZ are dispensable for SC proliferation after injury but required for remyelination of regenerated axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for remyelination of regenerated axons.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that YAP/TAZ are dispensable for SC proliferation after injury but required for remyelination of regenerated axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SCs are dependent on axons for their transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ.
source: These findings extend the role of YAP/TAZ to functional regeneration of injured nerves and suggest that SCs are dependent on axons for their transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' experimental observations.

claim: At one dpi when distal axons remained largely intact, nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ in associated SCs was unchanged.
source: At one dpi when distal axons remained largely intact, nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ in associated SCs was unchanged (Figure 1B; 1D-dstl).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At three dpi when axon degeneration was robust and SCs lost axon contacts, YAP/TAZ were almost undetectable in SC nuclei.
source: Strikingly, at three dpi when axon degeneration was robust and SCs lost axon contacts, YAP/TAZ were almost undetectable in SC nuclei (Figure 1B; 3D-dstl).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SCs lose nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ as associated axons degenerate.
source: Thus, SCs lose nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ as associated axons degenerate.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' observations from immunohistochemical data.

claim: YAP/TAZ reappeared in the nuclei of SCs at 6 dpi, and these SCs were associated with regenerating axons.
source: YAP/TAZ reappeared in the nuclei of SCs at 6 dpi, and these SCs were associated with regenerating axons (Figure 1B; 6D-dstl).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: By 12 dpi, as axon regeneration and maturation progressed further, more SCs exhibited strong nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ, comparable to that of SCs in the proximal neve stumps.
source: By 12 dpi, as axon regeneration and maturation progressed further, more SCs exhibited strong nuclear expression of YAP/TAZ, comparable to that of SCs in the proximal neve stumps (Figure 1B; 12D-dstl, see also Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1A.

claim: SCs upregulate nuclear YAP/TAZ when they regain axon contacts as axons regenerate.
source: These observations suggest that SCs upregulate nuclear YAP/TAZ, when they regain axon contacts as axons regenerate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: Thin regenerating axons associated with SCs at 3dpi do not have detectable YAP/TAZ in these SCs.
source: Notably, we frequently observed thin regenerating axons associated with SCs at 3dpi, but YAP/TAZ were undetectable in these SCs (Figure 1B; zoomed area of 3D-dstl).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SCs exhibiting strong YAP/TAZ at 6- and 12 dpi were associated with thick axons, which appeared large enough to be myelinated.
source: In contrast, SCs exhibiting strong YAP/TAZ at 6- and 12 dpi were associated with thick axons, which appeared large enough to be myelinated (i.e., 1>μm; Figure 1B; 6D-dstl, zoomed area of 12D-dstl).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YAP/TAZ are selectively upregulated in SCs associated with regenerating axons that have become large enough to be myelinated.
source: These observations suggest that YAP/TAZ are selectively upregulated in SCs associated with regenerating axons that have become large enough to be myelinated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: Western blotting revealed marked reduction of YAP and TAZ levels at 3 dpi, followed by rapid upregulation of TAZ levels.
source: Western blotting also revealed marked reduction of YAP and TAZ levels at 3 dpi, followed by rapid upregulation of TAZ levels (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YAP levels remained low in nerve lysates at 12 dpi.
source: Notably, YAP levels remained low in nerve lysates at 12 dpi (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YAP is upregulated in many SC nuclei at 6 dpi and continues to be observed at 24 dpi.
source: YAP is upregulated in many SC nuclei at 6 dpi and continues to be observed at 24 dpi (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YAP is upregulated in SCs concomitant with axon regeneration.
source: demonstrating that YAP is also upregulated in SCs concomitant with axon regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' immunohistochemical observations.

claim: The dramatic down- and upregulation of YAP/TAZ concurrent with axon degeneration and regeneration suggest that SCs are dependent on axons for YAP/TAZ nuclear expression.
source: The dramatic down- and upregulation of YAP/TAZ concurrent with axon degeneration and regeneration, respectively, suggest that SCs are dependent on axons for YAP/TAZ nuclear expression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ become undetectable in SCs at 3 dpi in transected nerves, concurrent with robust axon degeneration.
source: We first confirmed absence of regenerating axons in distal nerve stumps of these mice and found that YAP/TAZ become undetectable in SCs at 3 dpi (Figure 2B; 3D-dstl), concurrent with robust axon degeneration as observed after nerve crush injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nuclear YAP/TAZ continued to be undetectable in SCs after 3 dpi in transected nerves.
source: Notably, nuclear YAP/TAZ continued to be undetectable in SCs after 3 dpi (Figure 2B; e.g., 12D-dstl, see also Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2A.

claim: Axons are required for YAP/TAZ upregulation in denervated SCs.
source: demonstrating that axons are required for YAP/TAZ upregulation in denervated SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations in transected nerves.

claim: p-YAP became undetectable in SCs of transected/tied nerves by 12 dpi.
source: We found that p-YAP became undetectable in SCs of transected/tied nerves by 12 dpi (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: p-YAP expression recovered in SCs of crushed nerves at 12 dpi.
source: In contrast, p-YAP expression recovered in SCs of crushed nerves at 12 dpi (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SCs are dependent on axons for both nuclear and cytoplasmic expression of YAP/TAZ.
source: These findings suggest that SCs are dependent on axons for both nuclear and cytoplasmic expression of YAP/TAZ.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: SCs rapidly dedifferentiate and convert to repair SCs after nerve injury.
source: SCs rapidly dedifferentiate and convert to repair SCs after nerve injury.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Schwann cell behavior after injury.

claim: During transdifferentiation to repair SCs, SCs begin to proliferate ~3 dpi.
source: During this transdifferentiation process, SCs begin to proliferate ~3 dpi (Clemence et al., 1989; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Tricaud and Park, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Clemence et al., 1989; Jessen and Mirsky, 2016; Tricaud and Park, 2017).

claim: Pulse labeling with EdU indicated that the transected nerves of WT and iDKO contained similar numbers of dividing SCs in S phase.
source: Notably, pulse labeling with EdU indicated that the transected nerves of WT and iDKO contained similar numbers of dividing SCs in S phase (Figure 3C and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3C and quantified in Figure 3G.

claim: Numbers of Ki67+ proliferating SCs were similar in the transected nerves of WT and iDKO.
source: Numbers of Ki67+ proliferating SCs (Figure 3D and H) and of total SCs (Figure 3E and I) were also similar in the transected nerves of WT and iDKO.
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D and quantified in Figure 3H.

claim: Numbers of total SCs were similar in the transected nerves of WT and iDKO.
source: Numbers of Ki67+ proliferating SCs (Figure 3D and H) and of total SCs (Figure 3E and I) were also similar in the transected nerves of WT and iDKO.
evidence: The claim is supported by Sox10 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E and quantified in Figure 3I.

claim: Contralateral iDKO nerves contained neither EdU+ SCs nor apoptotic SCs at 12 dpi.
source: Contralateral iDKO nerves contained neither EdU+ SCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) nor apoptotic SCs, as assessed by TUNEL assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling and TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: SC numbers did not differ significantly between intact nerves of WT and iDKO mice at 12 dpi.
source: We also found that SC numbers did not differ significantly from those in intact nerves of WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sox10 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: YAP/TAZ do not regulate SC proliferation after nerve injury.
source: Collectively, these results strongly indicate that YAP/TAZ do not regulate SC proliferation after nerve injury.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data showing similar SC proliferation in WT and iDKO mice.

claim: c-Jun, pc-Jun, p75 NTR and Oct-6 were all upregulated in denervated SCs of iDKO mice after nerve injury, as in WT mice.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of transected sciatic nerves at five dpi showed that cJun, pc-Jun, p75 NTR and Oct-6 were all upregulated in denervated SCs of iDKO mice after nerve injury, as in WT mice (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injured nerves of WT and iDKO mice contained similar numbers of SCs expressing c-Jun.
source: Notably, injured nerves of WT and iDKO mice contained similar numbers of SCs expressing c-Jun (Figure 4A and E) and active pc-Jun (Figure 4B and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4A and quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: Injured nerves of WT and iDKO mice contained similar numbers of SCs expressing active pc-Jun.
source: Notably, injured nerves of WT and iDKO mice contained similar numbers of SCs expressing c-Jun (Figure 4A and E) and active pc-Jun (Figure 4B and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4F.

claim: p75 NTR expression was strongly upregulated in iDKO SCs, as in WT SCs.
source: p75 NTR expression was also strongly upregulated in iDKO SCs, as in WT SCs (Figure 4C and G)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4G.

claim: Oct-6 expression in WT and iDKO SCs did not differ.
source: and Oct-6 expression in WT and iDKO SCs did not differ (Figure 4D and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4D and quantified in Figure 4H.

claim: Numerous axons reached ~4 mm distal to the crush site in iDKO, as in WT mice at 3 dpi.
source: Numerous axons reached ~4 mm distal to the crush site in iDKO, as in WT mice (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: There was no significant difference in axon density measured 2 mm distal to the crush between WT and iDKO at 3 dpi.
source: There was no significant difference in axon density measured 2 mm distal to the crush (Figure 6C–E), nor in the length of the longest axons (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of axon density shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was no significant difference in the length of the longest axons between WT and iDKO at 3 dpi.
source: There was no significant difference in axon density measured 2 mm distal to the crush (Figure 6C–E), nor in the length of the longest axons (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SCs lacking YAP/TAZ convert normally to repair SCs and support axon regeneration after injury.
source: Taken together, these results show that SCs lacking YAP/TAZ convert normally to repair SCs and support axon regeneration after injury.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data showing normal axon regeneration in iDKO mice.

claim: Developing SCs lacking YAP/TAZ arrest as promyelinating SCs, and are unable to initiate myelin formation.
source: We have previously reported that developing SCs lacking YAP/TAZ arrest as promyelinating SCs, and are therefore unable to initiate myelin formation (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Grove et al., 2017).

claim: There was strong expression of myelin basic protein (MBP) in the crushed nerves of WT mice at 12-13 dpi.
source: As expected, there was strong expression of myelin basic protein (MBP), a major structural component of the myelin sheath, in the crushed nerves of WT mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: MBP immunoreactivity was abundant in the contralateral, intact nerves of iDKO mice at 12-13 dpi.
source: MBP immunoreactivity was also abundant in the contralateral, intact nerves of iDKO mice (Figure 7A; bottom panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: iDKO crushed nerves revealed remarkably little, if any, MBP immunoreactivity at 12-13 dpi.
source: In contrast, iDKO crushed nerves revealed remarkably little, if any, MBP immunoreactivity (Figure 7A and C, see also Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for higher magnification images).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A and 7C.

claim: Semithin and ultrathin sections contained many myelinated axons in WT but almost none in iDKO crushed nerves at 12-13 dpi.
source: Consistent with this immunohistochemical analysis, semithin (Figure 7D) and ultrathin sections processed for EM (Figures 5E and 7E) contained many myelinated axons in WT but almost none in iDKO crushed nerves (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D, 7E, and quantified in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: iDKO SCs frequently surrounded and established a 1:1 relationship with large axons, but none of these axons exhibited a myelin sheath.
source: Moreover, iDKO SCs frequently surrounded and established a 1:1 relationship with large axons, but none of these axons exhibited a myelin sheath (Figures 5E and 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figures 5E and 7E.

claim: Adult SCs lacking YAP/TAZ fail to remyelinate axons because they arrest at the promyelinating stage after injury.
source: These findings suggest that adult SCs lacking YAP/TAZ fail to remyelinate axons because they arrest at the promyelinating stage after injury.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Expression of YAP, assessed by Western blotting, selectively increases after nerve injury in mutant nerves lacking Merlin in SCs, but not in WT nerves.
source: Mindos et al., 2017 recently reported that expression of YAP, assessed by Western blotting, selectively increases after nerve injury in mutant nerves lacking Merlin in SCs, but not in WT nerves, whereas TAZ increases in both WT and mutant nerves.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Mindos et al., 2017).

claim: TAZ increases after nerve injury in both WT and Merlin mutant nerves.
source: Mindos et al., 2017 recently reported that expression of YAP, assessed by Western blotting, selectively increases after nerve injury in mutant nerves lacking Merlin in SCs, but not in WT nerves, whereas TAZ increases in both WT and mutant nerves.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Mindos et al., 2017).

claim: Elevated YAP levels prevent axon regeneration and remyelination in Merlin mutants.
source: They also reported that elevated YAP levels prevent axon regeneration and remyelination, and that inactivation of YAP alone is sufficient to restore full functional recovery of the Merlin mutants (Mindos et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Mindos et al., 2017).

claim: Inactivation of YAP alone is sufficient to restore full functional recovery of the Merlin mutants.
source: They also reported that elevated YAP levels prevent axon regeneration and remyelination, and that inactivation of YAP alone is sufficient to restore full functional recovery of the Merlin mutants (Mindos et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Mindos et al., 2017).

claim: Regenerating axons were as thick and numerous in Taz iKO, as in WT mice at 12 dpi.
source: We found that regenerating axons were as thick and numerous in Taz iKO, as in WT mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Axon density measured at 8 ~ 10 mm distal to the crush site showed no significant difference among WT, Taz iKO and Yap/Taz iDKO nerves at 12 dpi.
source: Axon density measured at 8 ~ 10 mm distal to the crush site showed no significant difference among WT, Taz iKO and Yap/Taz iDKO nerves (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of axon density shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Myelinated axons were frequent in Taz iKO nerves at 12 dpi.
source: We also found that, whereas iDKO nerves contained no myelinated axons (e.g., Figure 7D), myelinated axons were frequent in Taz iKO nerves (Figure 8C and F)
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 8C and quantified in Figure 8F.

claim: G-ratios did not differ in Taz iKO and WT at 12 dpi.
source: and G-ratios did not differ in Taz iKO and WT (Figure 8G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of G-ratios shown in Figure 8G.

claim: SCs expressing only YAP were capable of myelinating regenerated axons.
source: demonstrating that SCs expressing only YAP were capable of myelinating regenerated axons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations in Taz iKO mice.

claim: A significantly smaller percentage of single axons were myelinated in Taz iKO than in WT at 12 dpi.
source: Notably, however, a significantly smaller percentage of single axons were myelinated in Taz iKO than in WT (Figure 8F)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Remyelination is less advanced in Taz iKO nerves whose SCs express only YAP.
source: indicating that remyelination is less advanced in Taz iKO nerves whose SCs express only YAP.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the quantification data.

claim: YAP, at normal levels, does not prevent axon regeneration or remyelination after injury.
source: Taken together, these results show that YAP, at normal levels (see Discussion), does not prevent axon regeneration or remyelination after injury, and that both YAP and TAZ are required for optimal remyelination.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data in Taz iKO mice.

claim: Both YAP and TAZ are required for optimal remyelination.
source: Taken together, these results show that YAP, at normal levels (see Discussion), does not prevent axon regeneration or remyelination after injury, and that both YAP and TAZ are required for optimal remyelination.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data comparing WT, Taz iKO, and Yap/Taz iDKO mice.

claim: The number of c-Jun+ SCs was markedly, but similarly, reduced in nerves of both WT and iDKO at 12 dpi.
source: The number of c-Jun+ SCs was markedly, but similarly, reduced in nerves of both WT and iDKO at 12 dpi (Figure 9A,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9A and quantified in Figure 9E.

claim: Proliferating SCs were rare in both WT and iDKO nerves at 12 dpi.
source: and proliferating SCs were rare (Figure 9B,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9B and quantified in Figure 9F.

claim: Oct-6 expression was reduced in both WT and iDKO at 12 dpi, although it remained statistically higher in iDKO SCs.
source: Oct-6 expression was also reduced in both WT and iDKO (Figure 9C,G), although it remained statistically higher in iDKO SCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9C and quantified in Figure 9G.

claim: iDKO SCs are capable of downregulating dedifferentiation genes and withdraw gradually from dedifferentiation as like WT SCs.
source: These results suggest that iDKO SCs are capable of downregulating dedifferentiation genes and withdraw gradually from dedifferentiation as like WT SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: WT SCs upregulated Krox 20 expression at 12 dpi, concomitant with remyelination.
source: Notably, whereas WT SCs upregulated Krox 20 expression at 12 dpi, concomitant with remyelination, few if any iDKO SCs exhibited Krox 20 immunoreactivity (Figure 9D,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9D and quantified in Figure 9H.

claim: Few if any iDKO SCs exhibited Krox 20 immunoreactivity at 12 dpi.
source: Notably, whereas WT SCs upregulated Krox 20 expression at 12 dpi, concomitant with remyelination, few if any iDKO SCs exhibited Krox 20 immunoreactivity (Figure 9D,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9D and quantified in Figure 9H.

claim: iDKO SCs fail to myelinate regenerated axons at least in part due to failure to upregulate Krox 20.
source: These results suggest that iDKO SCs fail to myelinate regenerated axons at least in part due to failure to upregulate Krox 20.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for mature SCs to restore peripheral myelination after nerve injury.
source: Here we show that YAP/TAZ are required for mature SCs to restore peripheral myelination, but not to proliferate, after nerve injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: YAP/TAZ are not required for mature SCs to proliferate after nerve injury.
source: Here we show that YAP/TAZ are required for mature SCs to restore peripheral myelination, but not to proliferate, after nerve injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: YAP/TAZ ablation does not impair SC proliferation or transdifferentiation into growth promoting repair SCs.
source: YAP/TAZ ablation does not impair SC proliferation or transdifferentiation into growth promoting repair SCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SCs lacking YAP/TAZ fail to upregulate myelin-associated genes and completely fail to remyelinate regenerated axons.
source: SCs lacking YAP/TAZ, however, fail to upregulate myelin-associated genes and completely fail to remyelinate regenerated axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both YAP and TAZ are redundantly required for optimal remyelination.
source: We also show that both YAP and TAZ are redundantly required for optimal remyelination.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data comparing Taz iKO and Yap/Taz iDKO mice.

claim: Axons regulate transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ in adult SCs.
source: These findings suggest that axons regulate transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ in adult SCs and that YAP/TAZ are essential for functional regeneration of peripheral nerve.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations of axon-dependent YAP/TAZ expression.

claim: YAP/TAZ are essential for functional regeneration of peripheral nerve.
source: These findings suggest that axons regulate transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ in adult SCs and that YAP/TAZ are essential for functional regeneration of peripheral nerve.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations showing remyelination failure in iDKO mice.

claim: The nerve crush model evokes active axon degeneration in the distal nerve stump, while permitting new axons from the proximal nerve stump to regenerate through the crushed site within 1–2 days post injury.
source: The nerve crush model evokes active axon degeneration in the distal nerve stump, while permitting new axons from the proximal nerve stump to regenerate through the crushed site within 1–2 days post injury (dpi) (Kang and Lichtman, 2013; Jang et al., 2016; Frendo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Kang and Lichtman, 2013; Jang et al., 2016; Frendo et al., 2019).

claim: New axons regenerate within the basal lamina tubes filled with SCs and their processes, at the speed of 1–4 mm/day.
source: New axons then keep regenerating within the basal lamina tubes filled with SCs and their processes, at the speed of 1–4 mm/day, although the debris of degenerating axons and myelin is not yet completely removed.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about axon regeneration after nerve injury.

claim: Transcription of Krox 20 and other myelin genes remains robust in SCs up until two dpi, but is downregulated by three dpi.
source: In accordance with these ideas, transcription of Krox 20 and other myelin genes remains robust in SCs up until two dpi, but is downregulated by three dpi (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017).

claim: In mutant mice lacking Merlin, YAP is abnormally upregulated in SCs after nerve injury, impairing SC de-differentiation.
source: In support of this notion, in mutant mice lacking Merlin, YAP is abnormally upregulated in SCs after nerve injury, impairing SC de-differentiation (Mindos et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Mindos et al., 2017).

claim: One role of Merlin is to downregulate YAP in SCs.
source: This YAP upregulation suggests that one role of Merlin is to downregulate YAP in SCs and that YAP/TAZ expression in SCs is likely under active, presumably axon-dependent, regulation in both intact and injured mature nerves.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from observations in Merlin mutants.

claim: YAP/TAZ expression in SCs is likely under active, presumably axon-dependent, regulation in both intact and injured mature nerves.
source: This YAP upregulation suggests that one role of Merlin is to downregulate YAP in SCs and that YAP/TAZ expression in SCs is likely under active, presumably axon-dependent, regulation in both intact and injured mature nerves.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations and published data.

claim: Krox 20 is widely accepted as the key transcription factor promoting peripheral myelination.
source: Krox 20 is widely accepted as the key transcription factor promoting peripheral myelination.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Krox 20 is believed to be important for remyelination after injury.
source: This is largely believed to be the case after injury (Brügger et al., 2017), although its role in remyelination has never been explicitly demonstrated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Brügger et al., 2017), but the authors note it has not been explicitly demonstrated.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 complex directly binds to the cis-acting regulatory sequence of Krox 20 designated as the Myelinating Schwann cell Element (MSE) to upregulate Krox 20 during developmental myelination.
source: First, we and others demonstrated that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 complex directly binds to the cis-acting regulatory sequence of Krox 20 designated as the Myelinating Schwann cell Element (MSE) to upregulate Krox 20 during developmental myelination (Lopez-Anido et al., 2016; Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Lopez-Anido et al., 2016; Grove et al., 2017).

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 also bind to Krox 20 MSE in adult nerve.
source: Second, we showed that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 also bind to Krox 20 MSE in adult nerve, suggesting direct regulation of Krox 20 by YAP/TAZ in mature SCs (Grove et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Grove et al., 2017).

claim: Oct 6 induces upregulation of Krox 20, together with other TFs.
source: Third, Oct 6, which induces upregulation of Krox 20, together with other TFs, is upregulated in iDKO after nerve injury, as in WT (Figures 4H and 9G).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and supported by the authors' data shown in Figures 4H and 9G.

claim: Remyelination in iDKO is blocked at the step of Krox 20 upregulation.
source: This finding suggests that remyelination in iDKO is blocked at the step of Krox 20 upregulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations.

claim: iDKO SCs are arrested at the promyelination stage during development.
source: Indeed, we and others have shown that iDKO SCs are arrested at the promyelination stage during development (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Deng et al., 2017; Grove et al., 2017).

claim: After nerve injury, iDKO SCs proceed to the promyelination stage but fail to upregulate Krox 20 and initiate myelin formation.
source: and we found that, similarly after nerve injury, iDKO SCs proceed to the promyelination stage but fail to upregulate Krox 20 and initiate myelin formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Repair SCs rapidly upregulate both YAP and TAZ as axons regenerate and expression persists as regeneration continues.
source: We observed that repair SCs rapidly upregulate both YAP and TAZ as axons regenerate and that expression persists as regeneration continues.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Axon regeneration is as robust in Taz iKO and Yap/Taz iDKO as in WT, but not noticeably enhanced.
source: We also found that axon regeneration is as robust in Taz iKO and Yap/Taz iDKO as in WT, but not noticeably enhanced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: At least normal levels of YAP do not prevent axon regeneration.
source: Given that YAP is not compensatorily upregulated in Taz iKO (Figure 8A), these results suggest that at least normal levels of YAP do not prevent axon regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' observations in Taz iKO mice.

claim: Overly robust upregulation of YAP may severely compromise axon regeneration because excessive levels of YAP/TAZ alter the growth-promoting ability of SCs and/or cause their tumorigenic proliferation.
source: However, overly robust upregulation of YAP, presumably as in Merlin mutants (Mindos et al., 2017), may severely compromise axon regeneration because excessive levels of YAP/TAZ alter the growth-promoting ability of SCs and/or cause their tumorigenic proliferation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published data and the authors' observations.

claim: The levels of YAP/TAZ may be a critical determinant of their function in adult SCs.
source: The present study, together with earlier work, strongly suggests that the levels of YAP/TAZ may be a critical determinant of their function in adult SCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the authors' study and previous work.

claim: Optimal levels of YAP/TAZ promote myelin formation, maintenance and remyelination.
source: Optimal levels of YAP/TAZ promote myelin formation, maintenance and remyelination, whereas their absence promotes demyelination.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data and previous work.

claim: Absence of YAP/TAZ promotes demyelination.
source: Optimal levels of YAP/TAZ promote myelin formation, maintenance and remyelination, whereas their absence promotes demyelination.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' experimental data and previous work.

claim: Overly excessive levels of YAP/TAZ promote SC proliferation.
source: In contrast, overly excessive levels of YAP/TAZ promote SC proliferation.
